questions.q: What does MERGE combine into a single statement?
options: SELECT and WHERE only
CREATE and DROP
JOIN and GROUP BY
Insert, update, and delete
questions.explain: MERGE replaces what would otherwise require three separate statements with matching logic.

questions.q: What does WHEN MATCHED correspond to, and what action does it typically take?
options: The row exists only in target — typically DELETE
It always deletes the row regardless of match status
The row exists in both target and source (like INNER JOIN) — typically UPDATE
The row exists only in source — typically INSERT
questions.explain: WHEN MATCHED mirrors INNER JOIN's match logic from Lesson 22.

questions.q: What does WHEN NOT MATCHED BY TARGET mean?
options: The row exists in neither table
The row exists in source but not target — typically handled with INSERT
The row's data types don't match
The row exists in target but not source
questions.explain: This is the 'new row that needs to be added' scenario.

questions.q: What does WHEN NOT MATCHED BY SOURCE mean?
options: The source table doesn't exist
The row exists in target but not source — often handled with DELETE
The row exists in source but not target
The row was matched twice
questions.explain: This is the 'row that no longer belongs' scenario — often used to remove discontinued/stale rows.

questions.q: Why is MERGE the standard tool for loading a data warehouse?
options: It syncs a staging table's fresh data into a permanent table — updating changes, inserting new rows, all in one atomic statement
MERGE automatically creates the warehouse schema
MERGE is required syntax for any GROUP BY query
MERGE can only be used with data warehouse tables, never OLTP tables
questions.explain: This is previewed here and covered properly in Chapter 12's data warehousing content.
